title: Synthetic Linguistic Agency: How an Embodied Mortal Agent Learns Linguistic Affordances through Consequential Social Experience
one_sentence: A simulated mortal agent learns partner-sensitive linguistic actions through a causal body–utterance–partner-response–consequence loop whose effects persist in its social biography.
problem: Can language use become a consequential, body-conditioned capability rather than a detached text policy?
method: Simulated Embodied Mortal Agent with nonresetting health, fixed linguistic action choices, scripted partners, reinforcement learning, held-out biography tests, forced-output probes, and mortal/reset controls.
findings: Body state and accumulated social history jointly altered later linguistic action policies and partner-specific response choices.

Correct person-specific evidence improved action probability by roughly .356–.377 and produced positive remaining-useful-life and lifetime effects; reset controls removed the persistent next-turn body effect.
real_contribution: Operationalizes a consequential feedback chain connecting embodiment, linguistic action, partner response, and later adaptation.
biggest_weakness: One scripted simulated ecology, a one-dimensional declining body, four fixed actions, no human participants, and no open negotiation or repair.
claim_boundary: Shows history-conditioned partner-mediated adaptation, not common ground, mutual convention, natural-language emergence, physical embodiment, or human social interpretation.
why_researcher_should_care: Offers a causal design vocabulary for separating memory of interaction from consequences that actually change later communicative policy.
evidence_notes: Open arXiv HTML/PDF inspected; v1 submitted 2026-08-28.
Artificial sense-making is treated as a contested interpretation, not an established human analogue.
